text: This closes out the lock cluster of this chapter with the practical side: what to actually do about deadlocks, both preventing them and handling the ones that still happen.

The single biggest technique, by a wide margin, is accessing objects in a consistent order. Last lesson's deadlock happened because one session updated 680 then 681, and the other updated 681 then 680 — opposite orders. If every transaction in the system always touches these rows in the same order, that specific cyclical wait simply can't form.

Three more standard mitigations help too. Keep transactions short, since the longer a lock is held, the longer the window for a conflict. Use the lightest isolation level that still gives you the correctness you actually need — the next several lessons cover that in depth. And add helpful indexes, since lock duration correlates with scan time.
Even with all of that in place, error 1205 is expected to happen occasionally in a busy, well-designed system under real concurrent load. It isn't, by itself, evidence of broken code.

So the standard response lives in application code: a retry loop. Catch error 1205 specifically using ERROR_NUMBER, roll back if needed, and simply resubmit the same transaction from the top. That's the expected, correct way to handle a deadlock victim.

That's the full locking picture — shared, exclusive, update, intent, schema locks, granularity, escalation, viewing locks, and deadlocks. Next up, this chapter turns to isolation levels: exactly how much of this locking behavior you can relax, and what you give up each time you do.
